title: JSON support
description: All four engines store and query JSON, but indexing strategy and function names differ significantly.

migration.equivalent: Storing documents and extracting scalar values is conceptually identical across all four engines.
migration.different: Index strategy differs the most: PostgreSQL jsonb indexes the whole document with GIN, while SQL Server and MySQL require promoting paths to (computed/generated) columns.
migration.directMigration: Partial. Data migrates cleanly; queries and index DDL must be rewritten per engine.
migration.syntaxChanges: Replace JSON_VALUE/OPENJSON with the target engine's operators (->>, JSON_TABLE, jsonb_array_elements).
migration.limitations: SQL Server's native json type is 2025-only; older targets need nvarchar(max) + ISJSON.
migration.whenToUse: Use jsonb (PostgreSQL) when you need flexible ad-hoc indexing of documents; use the native json types elsewhere when documents are read via known paths.

title: Identity and sequence generation
description: Every engine auto-generates keys but the syntax and defaults differ.

migration.different: MySQL has no standalone SEQUENCE object; PostgreSQL/Oracle/SQL Server do.
migration.directMigration: Mostly yes for auto-increment; sequence-based designs need rework on MySQL.
migration.syntaxChanges: Replace NEXT VALUE FOR with nextval()/NEXTVAL; replace IDENTITY with AUTO_INCREMENT or GENERATED AS IDENTITY.
migration.limitations: MySQL emulates sequences via AUTO_INCREMENT or a helper table.
migration.whenToUse: Use SEQUENCE for cross-table keys or pre-fetching IDs; IDENTITY for simple cases.

title: Row-level security
description: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and Oracle enforce RLS in-engine; MySQL relies on views.

code.sqlserver: ADD FILTER PREDICATE sec.fn_tenant(TenantId) ON dbo.Orders;
code.postgresql: CREATE POLICY p ON orders USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int);
code.mysql: CREATE VIEW my_orders AS SELECT * FROM orders WHERE tenant_id = @app_tenant_id;

migration.equivalent: SQL Server FILTER/BLOCK maps almost 1:1 to PostgreSQL USING/WITH CHECK and to Oracle VPD.
migration.different: MySQL has no engine-level RLS; you must emulate with views and revoke base-table access.
migration.directMigration: Yes to PostgreSQL/Oracle with predicate rewrites; MySQL requires a view-based redesign.
migration.syntaxChanges: Rewrite the predicate function and swap SESSION_CONTEXT for current_setting/SYS_CONTEXT.
migration.limitations: MySQL's view approach is bypassable if users retain base-table privileges.
migration.whenToUse: Use native RLS wherever available; on MySQL, layer views plus strict grants.

title: Vector and AI capabilities
description: All four now offer vector types and ANN indexing; SQL Server and Oracle are closest in syntax, PostgreSQL uses pgvector operators, MySQL is the least mature for open-source ANN.

code.sqlserver: SELECT TOP 5 DocId FROM dbo.Doc ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', Embedding, @q);
code.postgresql: SELECT doc_id FROM doc ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5;
code.mysql: SELECT doc_id FROM doc ORDER BY DISTANCE(embedding, VEC_FROM_TEXT(?), 'COSINE') LIMIT 5;
code.oracle: SELECT doc_id FROM doc ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE(embedding, :q, COSINE) FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;

migration.equivalent: The store-embedding / order-by-distance pattern is identical everywhere.
migration.different: Index types (DiskANN vs HNSW/IVFFlat) and function vs operator syntax differ; MySQL open-source ANN is the weakest.
migration.directMigration: Yes for the query pattern; index DDL and distance syntax must be rewritten.
migration.syntaxChanges: Swap VECTOR_DISTANCE for pgvector operators or MySQL DISTANCE(); change index creation syntax.
migration.limitations: SQL Server DiskANN and several vector functions are in preview; MySQL open-source lacks mature ANN indexing.
migration.whenToUse: Choose the engine already holding your relational data so you avoid moving it — the core DP-800 value proposition.
